source_read: PDF, all 19 pages of the online-first PDF read in full; the article has no journal pagination, so pages are cited as p. N of the online-first PDF. Table 1 spans pp. 4-5 and was read in the text layer (fonts embedded, no scanning errors)

claims.overstatement: No. The claim takes nothing from this review as a finding of its own, and does not use the review's figures for the headline numbers. One thing the claim could add: this review's narrative attaches the 93% figure to an intramuscular dose of 2 to 4 mg/kg (p. 13), several times the 0.5 mg/kg at which it was measured, so a reader of the review alone would take the figure for a different condition.
claims.note: This source qualifies rather than establishes the claim. Its Table 1 (pp. 4-5) reproduces the 1982 values, with three differences worth recording: the oral bioavailability is printed as 17 rather than 16.6%; the intravenous row is given as n = 5 and cited to Clements and Nimmo (1981), while the intramuscular and oral rows are given as n = 6 and cited to Grant et al. (1981), so neither row is attributed to Clements et al. (1982) itself; and half-lives are converted to hours (3.1, 2.6 and 2.9 h for the intravenous, intramuscular and oral conditions, matching 186, 155 and 174 min). The review's own summary figures for swallowing (17 to 24% for racemic ketamine, 8 to 11% for oral S-ketamine, p. 12; 8 to 24% in the Key Points on p. 2 and the Summary on p. 14) are consistent with the claim's 16.6 to 19.5%, and the review gives a time to peak after swallowing of about 40 to 55 minutes (p. 12), later than the 30 minutes measured in 1982.

anchors.extracted: The review states that after an intramuscular dose of 2 to 4 mg/kg ketamine is rapidly absorbed with a bioavailability of approximately 93%, citing Grant et al. (1981) and Clements et al. (1982); that the terminal half-life after the intramuscular route does not differ significantly from the intravenous one; and that ketamine can be detected in plasma after 4 minutes with concentrations peaking 5 to 30 minutes after injection. The 93% figure was measured at 0.5 mg/kg, not at 2 to 4 mg/kg, and the review does not say so.

anchors.locator: Table 1, the first three data rows (Keta iv 0.25 mg/kg; Keta im 0.5 mg/kg; Keta po 0.5 mg/kg) with footnotes a and b
anchors.extracted: The review reproduces the 1982 values: intravenous 0.25 mg/kg, n = 5, area 27.5 (1.2), half-life 3.1 (0.1) h, cited to reference 87 (Clements and Nimmo 1981); intramuscular 0.5 mg/kg, n = 6, peak 243 (49) ng/mL at 22 (4) min, half-life 2.6 (0.1) h, cited to reference 10 (Grant et al. 1981); oral 0.5 mg/kg, n = 6, peak 44 (10) ng/mL at 30 (5) min, half-life 2.9 (0.8) h, bioavailability printed as 17%, same citation. Footnote b says these are mean and standard error and footnote a that areas are corrected to a 0.5 mg/kg dose. The oral figure is rounded from 16.6%, and no row is attributed to Clements et al. (1982).

The review states that only 17 to 24% of oral racemic ketamine and 8 to 11% of oral S-ketamine reach the systemic circulation, citing six sources, and that peak concentrations are reached about 40 to 55 minutes after swallowing with metabolites measurable after 10 to 30 minutes.

claims.overstatement: The claim says the review carries the rectal and nasal figures forward 'without their sample size'. That is true of the narrative sections (pp. 13) but not of the review as a whole: Table 1 on pp. 4-5 prints n = 3 for every one of the Yanagihara rows, next to the same figures. The rest of the sentence is accurate: the review's narrative gives approximately 30% rectal and approximately 45% nasal, second-hand, with no sample size, no dispersion and no mention of the swallowed sublingual tablets or the missing bowel preparation.
claims.note: This source is cited in the claim only for the sentence about the review carrying the figures forward. The review's nasal section also adds a time-to-peak range of 10 to 17 minutes attributed to the same two sources, which is narrower than, and not the same as, the 17.5 to 22.5 minutes printed in the primary study's table, and it states that norketamine exposure stays low after nasal administration, which does match the primary data.

anchors.locator: 7.5 Nasal Ketamine, 1st paragraph, and 7.6 Rectal Ketamine, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The review states that the bioavailability of the nasal spray is approximately 45%, slightly greater than sublingual, rectal and especially oral administration, that peak concentrations are reached rapidly (10 to 17 minutes) and that norketamine exposure remains low because of weak first-pass metabolism; and that with rectal administration bioavailability is approximately 30% and the norketamine area very similar to the sublingual tablet. Both passages cite only reference numbers; no sample size, dispersion or study condition is given, and neither the swallowing of the sublingual tablets nor the absent bowel preparation is mentioned.

anchors.locator: Table 1, the Keta sl 50 mg, Keta pr 50 mg and Keta in 25 mg rows with footnote c
anchors.extracted: The same study's values are printed in the review's table with n = 3 stated for each preparation and with the primary paper's means and standard deviations (for example nasal 25 mg: peak 29.4 (16.5) and 29.3 (13.8) ng/mL, time to peak 22.5 (9.6) and 17.5 (5.0) min; norketamine areas 115.9 (17.6) and 100.7 (39.6) ng h/mL). Footnote d records that the norketamine areas run from baseline to 8 hours in healthy volunteers. So the review does print the sample size, in the table rather than in the text.

claims.overstatement: The claim's opening generalisation, that activity measured as glucose use, blood flow or the fMRI signal 'goes up rather than down', is wider than this source supports. The review reports, second-hand, that the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen and of glucose was virtually unaffected at an anaesthetic dose of S-ketamine while blood flow rose, and that low-dose racemic ketamine showed only a tendency to increase glucose metabolism and blood flow. Blood flow and glucose use came apart in the studies this review describes, so the three measures should not be run together in one direction.
claims.note: This source enters the claim as a single qualifying anchor and adds no primary data. Its numbers (36% and 13% increases in whole-brain cerebral blood flow at anaesthetic and subanaesthetic doses of S-ketamine) do not appear in the claim's statement or magnitude, so there is nothing further to recompute. The review's dose anchoring is clear (anaesthetic versus subanaesthetic) and is reported in healthy volunteers during administration, consistent with the claim's restriction to a single session with ketamine in the body.

anchors.locator: 6.3.2 Effects on Neurotoxicity, Neuroprotection, and Intracranial Pressure, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: The review reports from a positron emission tomography study in healthy volunteers that an anaesthetic dose of S-ketamine increased whole-brain cerebral blood flow by 36% and a subanaesthetic dose by 13%, while the metabolic rate of oxygen and glucose remained virtually unaffected, so that perfusion was abundant especially in the insula and anterior cingulate; and that a similar study with low-dose racemic ketamine showed a tendency to increase the glucose metabolic rate and cerebral blood flow in a dose-dependent manner. All of this is second-hand, with no sample size, dispersion or test statistic.

claims.overstatement: No. The claim marks every figure from this review as second-hand, keeps 'postulated' for the potency statement, and describes the side-effect difference only as a difference in what is reported, which is as much as the review supports. Two points it could sharpen: the fourfold affinity figure is the review's explanation of an analgesic potency difference and is attributed to a single 1992 source; and the review is internally inconsistent about which enantiomer has more psychotomimetic effects.
claims.note: All review-derived numbers in the claim were found and match. The clearance figures are reported by the review from a stereoselective study in ten healthy male volunteers given both the racemate and S-ketamine by computer-controlled infusion in randomised double-blind crossover: 26.3 mL/kg/min for S-ketamine alone against 18.5 mL/kg/min for the S-form inside the racemate (the review also prints 14.8 mL/kg/min for racemic ketamine, which the claim omits without distortion). The inconsistency on side effects is a reporting issue: p. 9 says the S(+)-enantiomer produces more auditory and visual disturbances than the R(-)-isomer, while the Abstract (p. 1) and the Summary (p. 14) say S-ketamine produces fewer psychomimetic adverse effects than the racemate and than R-ketamine. Nothing in this source bears on the Vollenweider scans or on the blind in that study.

anchors.locator: 6 Pharmacodynamics and Clinical Use, 2nd paragraph (continuing the section's opening text)
anchors.extracted: The review states that the two enantiomers have similar pharmacokinetic profiles but different effects; that some studies indicate the S(+)-enantiomer may be about four times more potent than the R(-)-isomer as an analgesic in humans while producing more auditory and visual disturbances; that R-ketamine produces more agitation in surgical patients; and that the difference in analgesic efficiency can be explained by S-ketamine's four times higher affinity for NMDA receptors in comparison with the R(-)-enantiomer, attributed to a single 1992 study.

The review reports that in ten healthy male volunteers given both the racemate and S-ketamine by a computer-controlled device in a randomised, double-blind, crossover setting, S-ketamine clearance was significantly higher when given alone (26.3 mL/kg/min) than racemic ketamine (14.8 mL/kg/min), and that the clearance of S-ketamine inside the racemate was lower (18.5 mL/kg/min) than when given as the pure isomer, which it reads as R-ketamine inhibiting the clearance of S-ketamine.

anchors.locator: Abstract, 1st paragraph, read with the Introduction on p. 2 and the Summary on p. 14
anchors.extracted: The abstract says the S(+)-enantiomer has been postulated to be a four times more potent anaesthetic and analgesic than the R(-)-enantiomer and approximately two times more effective than the racemic mixture, and that fewer psychomimetic adverse effects have been reported with S-ketamine than with the racemate; the Introduction repeats the two- and fourfold potency statement, and the Summary says S-ketamine produces fewer psychomimetic adverse effects than R-ketamine and the racemate, which sits against the statement on p. 9 that the S(+)-enantiomer produces more auditory and visual disturbances than the R(-)-isomer.

claims.overstatement: No. Every figure taken from this review is labelled second-hand in the claim, the norketamine conversion figure is given as the review's report rather than as a measurement, and the qualification that norketamine may not be the main circulating substance is carried over as the review states it.
claims.note: All four review-derived figures were found and match: a distribution half-life of 2 to 4 minutes and an elimination half-life of 2 to 4 hours (p. 3), 4 to 7 hours for S-ketamine (p. 6), about 80% of ketamine demethylated to norketamine, measurable in plasma 2 to 3 minutes after an intravenous bolus and peaking at 30 to 60 minutes (p. 7). The review itself is in tension on the metabolite: the same paragraph on p. 6 calls norketamine the major metabolite in humans and then reports that recent studies indicate it is rapidly further metabolised and is not the major metabolite in the circulation; a modelling study is cited for a norketamine elimination half-life of 1.1 h against 2.1 h for ketamine (p. 7). None of these figures is given with a sample size or an interval.

anchors.extracted: The review states that ketamine has a short alpha half-life of 2 to 4 minutes and a longer beta half-life of 2 to 4 hours in humans, citing two sources; plasma protein binding 10 to 30%; steady-state volume of distribution 160 to 550 L per 70 kg; systemic clearance 60 to 147 L/h per 70 kg, which it says equals liver blood flow and explains the low bioavailability after swallowing.

anchors.extracted: The elimination half-life of S-ketamine is said to be slightly longer, 4 to 7 hours, than that of the racemate. In the next paragraph norketamine is called the major metabolite in humans and pharmacologically active, and then recent studies are reported as indicating that norketamine is rapidly further metabolised and is not the major metabolite in the circulation.

anchors.locator: Section 4.1, 2nd and last paragraph, which begins on p. 6 and ends at the top of the left column of p. 7
anchors.extracted: About 80% of ketamine is reported to be N-demethylated to norketamine, which can be measured in plasma 2 to 3 minutes after an intravenous ketamine bolus, with the maximum plasma concentration reached after 30 to 60 minutes; two sources are cited and no sample size or dispersion is given.

anchors.locator: Table 1, rows for Keta iv/im/po 0.25-0.5 mg/kg and Keta iv 20 mg
anchors.extracted: The review's own table prints the half-lives the claim takes from the two primary studies, converted to hours: 3.1 (0.1), 2.6 (0.1) and 2.9 (0.8) h for the intravenous, intramuscular and oral conditions of the 1982 study, and 2.1 and 2.0 h for the (R)- and (S)-enantiomers after a 20 mg injection in three people, with no half-life printed for any of that study's other preparations.

key_findings.correction: The figures are right (17 to 24% racemic and 8 to 11% S-ketamine in Section 7.2 on p. 12; the combined 8 to 24% range), but not where the card puts them. The combined range appears in Section 1 Introduction (p. 2, right column, where the Introduction's text continues) and in Section 9 Summary (p. 14). The Abstract (p. 1) and the Key Points box (p. 2) make the point without any number ('oral bioavailability is poor', 'low oral bioavailability'). The note about sample sizes appearing only in Table 1 is correct.
Section 7.5 on p. 13 as given; the review's phrase for the last point is that the exact dosing of ketamine is difficult to control.
Section 4's first paragraph does begin on p. 3 and end at the top of p. 6, with Table 1 between; all six values verified.

Content confirmed, locator wrong: Section 4.1 has only two paragraphs. The first (p. 6) carries the metabolic pathway, the active metabolite, the recent finding that norketamine is not the major circulating metabolite, biliary and urinary excretion and the absence of interconversion; the second begins on p. 6 and ends at the top of p. 7 and carries the CYP work, including the 80% conversion and the 2 to 3 minute and 30 to 60 minute timings. So read '1st and 2nd paragraphs', not '1st and 3rd'.

Content confirmed, including that Figures 3 and 4 on p. 6 print 95% confidence intervals without numbers and that the five underlying studies are the authors' own. All the interaction text sits in Section 4.1's 2nd paragraph (pp. 6-7), not in a 3rd and 4th paragraph.
All six concentration figures verified in Section 6, 1st paragraph (p. 9); reference 85 is indeed a textbook chapter.

Every number is right (26.3 against 18.5 mL/kg/min in ten healthy male volunteers, with 14.8 for the racemate, which the card omits). Two locator corrections: the clearance passage is Section 4.2's 2nd paragraph on p. 7, not the 3rd; and the statement that there is no interconversion is in Section 4.1's 1st paragraph on p. 6, not in the Abstract or Section 6.

The 16.5-times figure is in Section 7.2 on p. 12, as the card says.
Section 6.4.1, 2nd paragraph, p. 11; all four figures verified.

Both statements confirmed. The cerebral blood flow paragraph begins on p. 11 and is the 5th paragraph of Section 6.3.2, not its last and not on p. 10: two further paragraphs of that section follow it, on status epilepticus and on intracranial pressure. reporting_issues.note: Verified against the 1982 paper, which I read for this round: every value in Table 1's first three rows matches its Table II, no row cites reference 11, and the table's reference column runs 87, 10, 10 for those rows.

My own conversion agrees: 155 minutes with a standard error of 12 is 2.6 h with 0.2, while the table prints 0.1; 186 with 8 gives 3.1 (0.1) and 174 with 50 gives 2.9 (0.8), both correct. Worth adding that the correct intravenous conversion shows the review took the standard error from the 1982 Table II (8 minutes) rather than from that paper's Results (10 minutes).
The bioavailability column is blank for the intramuscular row and for all five rows of the formulation study, and filled only in the five places the card lists.
Found independently in the blind reading.
Verified: 40.0 against 33.3 minutes for the (R)-enantiomer in the table's sublingual and oral rows from reference 12.
Verified across the table's oral rows: 42 to 54 minutes for oral S-ketamine, 30 (5) and 33.3/30.0 minutes for oral racemic ketamine, and 120 minutes in the patient study.

The point stands and the lower bound is right, but the upper one is understated: with hepatic blood flow at 1.53 L/min, that is 91.8 L/h, so 60 L/h is about a third below and 147 L/h about 60% above, not a half.
The first row reads 0,25 mg/kg and two later rows split the unit as 0.1 mg/k g and 0.2 mg/k g.
I confirm the PDF carries no printed page numbers over its 19 pages; I did not check the reference record for the printed volume and pages.

risk_of_bias.note: The editors' narrative-review checklist is the right instrument under METHODS section 5.3, the vocabulary is the checklist's own, the overall judgment is not less severe than the worst domain, and each domain judgment is supported by what I read. I agree in particular with the balance domain: harm occupies one short section of a nineteen-page review and contains no frequency for anything.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right, and the four specific gaps are all in the text. One correction inside the reasoning, the same one as for key finding 0: the numerical ranges (8 to 24%, about 45%) are not in the Abstract or the Key Points, which make the point qualitatively; they are in the Introduction (p. 2), Sections 7.2 and 7.5 (pp. 12-13) and the Summary (p. 14). The criticism is unaffected, since those places give the figures without sample sizes either.

missed: The review contradicts itself on which enantiomer produces more psychotomimetic effects. Section 6 on p. 9 says the S(+)-enantiomer is about four times more potent as an analgesic 'but it produces more auditory and visual disturbances' and that R-ketamine produces more agitation in surgical patients, while the Abstract (p. 1) and the Summary (p. 14) say S-ketamine produces fewer psychomimetic adverse effects than the racemate and than R-ketamine. Any claim about how the two forms differ in effects should not take a single sentence of this review as its support.

Section 4.1's first paragraph (p. 6) calls norketamine the major metabolite in humans and, three sentences later, reports that recent studies indicate it is not the major metabolite in the circulation, without resolving the two. Key finding 6 records both halves as one finding; the tension itself is the thing a claim has to carry.

Section 5.2 (p. 8) states that S-ketamine has 2 to 3 times higher affinity for opioid receptors than R-ketamine. That figure is easy to conflate with the fourfold NMDA affinity in Section 6, and a card that records only the latter leaves the trap open.
